transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-01-14 16:00 UTC / Duration ~47m / RecordingID: ff-20270114-velora-001
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jillian Wong (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood), Priya Raman (Velora Lead ML Eng), Carlos Mendes (Velora SRE), Dana Cho (Velora CTO)

00:00 Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I know we've got a packed agenda so we'll try to keep it tight. quick roll call — can you confirm you're seeing the shared dashboard?
00:07 Priya: yep can see the dashboards, the throughput run from last night, looks like you guys pushed a couple of config tweaks?
00:12 Jillian: yeah we bumped the max_batch up to 48 for that run and raised the batching window to 30ms to encourage continuous batching. also we lowered concurrency floor so the runtime could accumulate slightly larger prefix batches.
00:25 Carlos: i noticed the avg tokens/sec went up but p99 on some slices spiked — there was a tail around 1.1s which is above our target, trying to understand root cause.
00:34 Marcus: quick context — those tails are correlated with long context sessions (>=1500 tokens) and cache miss patterns, plus a couple of large embeddings calls that coincided. we saw KV cash misses — transcription artifact, meant KV cache — that caused regeneration of full attention.
00:48 Dana: ok but our primary goal for the pilot is steady-state user-facing responses: 200 rps sustained, p95 < 300ms, p99 < 700ms for a 512-token prompt. is that still feasible with the current batching strategy?
01:02 Jillian: short answer: yes, with tradeoffs. continuous batching gives better token efficiency but can add queuing latency for individual requests. we can tune by setting concurrency caps, max batch sizes, and a maximum batching delay (we used 30ms last night).
01:18 Priya: can you explain how concurrency cap interacts with batch assembly? i'm trying to map to our traffic where peaks are bursty at the top of the hour.
01:26 Jillian: sure — runtime has two levers: concurrency (how many outstanding in-flight prompts per worker) and batching window/size. if concurrency is high, requests get issued to many workers quickly which can reduce queueing per worker but also reduces batch formation, hurting throughput efficiency. lowering concurrency lets the batcher collect more requests up to max_batch, improving throughput but increasing per-request wait.
01:50 Samir: so it's a balance — when you want lower p99 you might reduce max_batch or decrease batching window, accept higher cost; when you want higher throughput and lower cost, increase batch and window, accept higher small-number tail latency.
02:06 Carlos: last night's run — what's the per-worker concurrency you set?
02:10 Jillian: set per-worker concurrency to 18 and concurrency cap at the orchestration level to 72 across the pod. that gave us a good throughput but produced the tail when KV cache misses aligned.
02:23 Priya: are KV cache misses predictable? can we pre-warm?
02:26 Marcus: partially. we use prefix caching for common system prompts; user-specific long-history isn't prewarmable without violating privacy. we can however push a small cache-warm front-run for session starters with anon buckets. but the big wins are tuning batch size and fallback routing: when cache miss occurs, route to a variant optimized for long-context with fewer attention overheads or quantized config.
02:46 Dana: route to fallback model variant — that's interesting. what's the throughput delta on those variants?
02:51 Jillian: the long-context variant is slightly slower per-token but has lower memory thrash; throughput is ~15% lower but p99 on long contexts improves because it's specialized. also fallback can be policy-driven — if queue depth > X, send to the faster short-context variant with truncation and append a 'resume' job to finish later.
03:14 Priya: we worry about truncating user context and breaking UX. any suggestions?
03:18 Marcus: a multi-stage approach: first, try KV-aware routing to the long-context variant; if the backlog pushes total latency above SLO, then apply safe truncation on non-critical parts (system messages), or offload history to an async followup. we can instrument flags to measure degradation.
03:41 Samir: quick data point from the replay — increasing max_batch from 32 to 48 improved tokens/sec by ~22% but increased median queue wait by ~18ms and added a small p99 delta for long contexts.
03:55 Carlos: okay that tracks. what about concurrency caps? any experiment where you lowered per-worker concurrency to 12?
04:00 Jillian: we ran a short test — per-worker concurrency 12, max_batch 64, batching window 40ms: throughput was similar, cost efficiency improved but median tail for short prompts actually dropped (because batches were fuller) yet some individual requests experienced extra queueing wait which showed in our user-observed p95s for interactive flows.
04:24 Priya: that seems like an acceptable trade if we can keep p99 below 700ms. which config hit that?
04:29 Jillian: the config that best aligned with your SLO was per-worker concurrency 16, max_batch 48, batching window 30ms, with KV cache prefetch heuristics enabled. that hit p95 ~ 280ms and p99 ~ 640ms on the 512-token distribution in the last run.
04:48 Dana: okay good. now about backlog shaping — can Redwood apply a queue aging policy? e.g., if a request sits for >150ms in queue, mark it 'latency-sensitive' and prioritize?
04:58 Marcus: we support priority tiers. you can tag requests as interactive vs batch. runtime will prefer interactive for batch assembly and can steal slots to reduce head-of-line blocking. we also have adaptive queue shaping that reduces max_batch when queue ages exceed threshold, to drain faster.
05:18 Priya: do we need SDK changes to mark interactive?
05:22 Jillian: minimal — header flag or annotation in request. we can provide a small patch for your client to set is_interactive. no big SDK rewrite.
05:31 Carlos: network jitter — our VPC peering has occasional 20-40ms spikes, do those affect batched assembly?
05:35 Marcus: yes, network jitter increases variance in arrival times and can reduce effective batch sizes causing more partial batches. if jitter is predominant, we recommend slightly larger batching window or client-side batching to smooth arrivals. also we can configure route affinity to lower network hops.
05:56 Samir: action item — we heard two asks: (a) run a longer replay with the recommended config and include long-context traces, (b) customer sends 72h traces. does that capture?
06:04 Priya: yes and also we want the deep-dive on quantization tradeoffs because cost difference matters to procurement.
06:09 Samir: noted — we'll schedule 30m deep-dive once replay results are in.
06:13 Jillian: one more note on fallback capacity — we can set a reserved slot pool on Dedicated to handle burst fallbacks, or if hosted, we can configure auto-burst which gives transient extra workers. there's a small overage cost but it's a good safety valve for latency SLOs.
06:31 Dana: procurement will want cost delta numbers. can you include burst overage costs and expected cost per 1M tokens for the recommended config?
06:38 Samir: yes i'll include a short costing appendix with the pilot pricing sheet.
06:42 Carlos: small transcription hiccup I noticed in the logs — function calls from our orchestration service sometimes retry which congests queue. we can look at client-side retry backoff.
06:51 Marcus: good catch — we recommend exponential jitter and client-side limit to concurrent retries, and server will dedupe identical request ids when possible.
07:02 Priya: curious about reclaiming KV cache space — eviction policy is LRU now? could we do per-customer pinned prefixes?
07:08 Jillian: eviction is LRU with some weighted retention for system prompts. we can support pinned prefixes for your tenant in a dedicated pool (requires Dedicated or private deployment), or we can approximate with hotlist pinning on hosted. pinning improves hit rates but has memory cost tradeoffs.
07:25 Dana: overall, I'm pleased — the current recommended config looks like it meets our SLOs with the caveat of KV miss mitigation. let's log next steps.
07:33 Samir: recap of next steps — Jillian run 2hr replay with config: per-worker concurrency 16, max_batch 48, batching window 30ms; enable KV prefetch heuristics. Priya provide 72h traces. Carlos validate VPC peering numbers and retry behavior. Samir to send pricing and burst cost. schedule quantization deep-dive.
07:54 Priya: quick question — what's the expected reduction in cost if we move to a quantized variant? ballpark percent.
07:59 Jillian: ballpark 15–30% depending on accuracy tolerance and model family; we'll quantify in the deep dive.
08:08 Dana: ok we'll prep internal stakeholders. thanks everyone.
08:12 Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with the replay results and book the quantization session. end.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional speaker swaps; 'KV cash' instead of KV cache; some acronyms mis-typed (VPCe). timestamps are approximate.

References mentioned: pilot benchmarking sheet (link: https://redwood.example/pilots/VELORA-43-benchmarks), security brief (link: https://redwood.example/security/hosted-sla), sample replay script (link: https://redwood.example/tools/replay-runner).
